title: How do you read stacked bar charts without missing the real story?
description: How to read stacked and 100% stacked bar charts in case interviews, avoid the classic misreadings, and find the segment that changed, with a worked example.
hook: Stacked bar charts are packed with information, which makes them easy to misread under pressure. The trick is to know which comparisons they make easy and which they hide.
body:
Two kinds

  • Stacked bars show totals, split into segments.
  • 100% stacked bars show only the shares of each segment, with every bar the same height.

A worked example

Revenue by channel over two years: stores £75M → £150M, online £40M → £36M, wholesale £90M → £99M. Total rose from £205M to £285M.

Insight: "Total revenue grew 39%, but almost all of it came from stores, which doubled. Online actually shrank 10%, a worrying sign if the client is investing in digital."

How to read one quickly

  1. Check whether it shows totals or shares.
  2. Compare totals first.
  3. Compare the bottom segment directly; it sits on the axis, so it is easy to read.
  4. For other segments, work out each one's size by subtraction, rather than guessing by eye.

Common traps

  • A 100% stacked chart can show a segment's share falling while its actual value grows.
  • Middle segments are hard to compare by eye; calculate them.
  • Missing the total and only describing the parts.

Separate a growing total from a changing mix

A stacked bar chart shows a company's revenue split between stores and online. In year one, stores contribute £60 million and online £40 million, for £100 million total. In year two, stores contribute £60 million and online £60 million, for £120 million total. Total revenue is up 20%, but every pound of growth came from online. Online's revenue share rose from 40% to 50%.

A 100%-stacked version of the same chart would show only the 40% to 50% share shift. It would not show that actual revenue rose by £20 million. It is therefore unsafe to say a segment's sales fell because its proportion got smaller. A category can lose share while growing in absolute terms if the total expands even faster.

Read a stacked chart in three passes: first the total heights, then the segment amounts or percentages, then the implication for the client's decision. If online orders have lower profit per pound because of returns and fulfilment, the changing mix may lower company margin even while sales grow.

Try it aloud: "The business grew 20%, but stores were flat and online generated all the increase. Before calling this good growth, I'd compare contribution margins by channel." The next dataset should show channel profit, not merely more revenue bars.
